name: Vera Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on twelve-hour shifts, four days and four nights, then four off. I drive a 240-tonne haul truck, number 47, from the shovel down to the crusher and back, maybe thirty loads a shift. I like the quiet up in the cab and the view over the pit at sunrise. What wears me out is nights, and the dust gets into everything, even my lunchbox.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and who do you work with?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Seven years now, since I finished my certificate at the tech college. I eat lunch with Gus, an old fitter who's been here thirty years and tells the same three stories. My partner Tomas is a nurse at the hospital in Redhill, so between his rosters and mine we sometimes only see each other on the driveway. The north pit, our sister site, already runs driverless trucks, so we all know what's coming eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, maybe the bosses will stop selling us a robot future and fix the air-conditioning in the trucks instead. At the union meeting I'd say this is the moment to lock in a decent agreement while they're not distracted. I don't post much online, but I'd share that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it doesn't change much for me, because the driverless trucks at the north pit aren't AI hype, they're already real. Those trucks were coming with or without some chatbot. So I'd still be looking over my shoulder, just a bit less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep my head down, same roster. I'd keep putting 400 a month into savings, because three months of bills isn't much if they move our pit to driverless. And I'd go to every union meeting this year, because the next agreement is the one that decides redundancy pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, but not relaxed. It's like a storm warning being cancelled when you can still see clouds over the north pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the driverless trucks were coming anyway. What would tell you they're coming to your pit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When they start putting GPS masts up on our benches, that's the sign, because that's how it started up north. Gus says they surveyed there for a full year before the first truck ran without a driver. If the survey crews show up on our benches with GPS masts, I'll know my truck has about a year left with me in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomas say if you came home with that news?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas would tell me to go back to study, because the hospital always needs people. But I'm not a needles person, and I don't want to start over at the bottom. I'd rather fight to keep the job I'm good at.

say: I'd tell the crew this is the time to **lock in** a strong union agreement.
I'd say the bosses should fix the **truck air-conditioning** instead of chasing robot dreams.
think: Driverless trucks at the **north pit** are already real, so AI hype barely matters to me.
My **job risk** comes from robots, not chatbots, and that risk hasn't gone away.
do: Keep driving truck 47 on the **same roster** and keep my head down.
Put **400 a month** into savings to grow my three-month cushion.
Attend every **union meeting** before the next agreement sets redundancy pay.
feel: Relieved, but **not relaxed**, because the north pit still runs **driverless trucks**.
S0.quote: If the survey crews show up on our benches with GPS masts, I'll know my truck has about a year left with me in it.
fieldNote: Her worry is about **robots**, which she sees as separate from AI hype.
She watches for **GPS masts** on the benches as the first sign of change.
The **union agreement** is her main lever, and she plans around it.

steps.text: Keep driving truck 47 on the four-on, four-off roster
Put 400 a month into the savings account
Go to every union meeting before the new agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at the lunch table straight out: the robots are slower, but they're still coming, and we need a deal now. I'd push the union to ask for retraining paid by the company, not by us. Online I'd share posts about taxing companies that cut jobs with machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the office people go first this time, the planners and the dispatchers who send us our loads. Dispatch is already half software. Once dispatch is all software, putting a truck on autopilot is the easy bit, so my job gets shorter too, maybe in five or six years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union's technology committee, even though meetings bore me. I'd bump my savings to 600 a month by cutting takeaway and the gym. I'd sign a petition for a law that makes mines pay for retraining when they automate, and I'd vote that way at the next election.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into worried. I'm 27, and I don't want my whole career to be a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI tools. Would that change if the company offered training on them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not unless they made it part of the job. I know that sounds stubborn. I'd rather learn to fix a haul truck than learn to babysit a computer that drives one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya in dispatch, because her whole job is on a screen and she's got a little boy. And Gus, honestly, because he's sixty and nobody retrains a sixty-year-old fitter for a software job. I'd worry about them before me.

say: I'd tell my crew the **robots are coming** slower, but we need a deal now.
I'd push the union for **company-paid retraining**, not training we pay for ourselves.
Online I'd share posts about **taxing companies** that replace workers with machines.
think: The **dispatchers** go first, because their work is already half software.
Once dispatch is software, a **driverless truck** is easy, so my job has maybe six years.
do: Join the union's **technology committee**, even though long meetings bore me.
Raise savings to **600 a month** by cutting takeaway and the gym.
Sign petitions and **vote** for laws making mines pay for retraining.
feel: **Uneasy** turning into worried, because my career starts to feel like a **countdown**.
S1.quote: I'd rather learn to fix a haul truck than learn to babysit a computer that drives one.
fieldNote: She expects **office roles** like dispatch to go first, then her truck.
She'd rather **learn a trade** than learn AI tools, a clear line she draws.
Her first worries are for **colleagues**: a sixty-year-old fitter and a dispatcher with a child.

steps.text: Join the union's technology committee this year
Cut takeaway and the gym to save 600 a month
Vote for laws making mines fund retraining when they automate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that this is exactly what the union has been warning about, and governments are asleep. I'd say the mine owners will get richer and towns like Redhill will empty out. I'd probably post that, and my mum would ask me to calm down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In my head I'd be doing the maths. Thinking AI by 2028 means dispatch and planning are gone straight away, and robots by 2031 means my cab is empty when I'm thirty-one. I'd be thirty-one with a truck licence for a truck that doesn't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Tomas and work out how long we could live on his pay alone, because hospitals change slowly. I'd stop the holiday we were saving for and put all of that into savings. I'd sell the pickup and take the mine bus. In the first year after it arrives I'd start a heavy diesel fitting apprenticeship if the union can get the company to pay, and I'd be at every rally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in my stomach, honestly. Three years sounds like a lot until you realise it's one agreement cycle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the warning time of 2 years change for you, compared with a slower picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's no time to finish a four-year apprenticeship before the robots come in 2031. So I'd be retraining into something that might also be automated by the time I'm qualified. That's the part that scares me, picking the wrong lifeboat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if your pay stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan, so the pickup goes first. Then the gym and the streaming stuff. Rent can't go, because Tomas and I signed a lease until 2028.

say: I'd say the union **warned about this** and governments are asleep.
I'd say owners get **richer** while towns like **Redhill** empty out.
think: Thinking AI ends **dispatch and planning** in 2028, before my own job goes.
Robots by **2031** mean my cab is empty when I'm thirty-one.
do: Work out with Tomas how long we'd live on **his pay alone**.
Move the **holiday fund** into savings and sell the pickup in month one.
Start a **diesel fitting apprenticeship** if the union gets the company to pay.
feel: **Sick** in my stomach, because three years is only one **agreement cycle**.
S2.quote: I'd be thirty-one with a truck licence for a truck that doesn't need me.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** before robots feels short to her, just one agreement.
She fears **picking the wrong** retraining path that also gets automated.
Her partner's **hospital job** is the household's safety net in her plans.

steps.text: Move the holiday fund into savings in the first month
Sell the pickup and take the mine bus to work
Start a diesel fitting apprenticeship if the company pays
March at union rallies for a fair transition deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, and I'd say it loudly at the union. I'd tell people this is the time to get a law for retraining and a proper redundancy fund. I'd say it's not the robots' fault, it's who owns them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years plus three for robots is 2034, and I'd be thirty-five. That's enough time to finish a trade if I start soon. But I'd still be hoping someone higher up sorts it out, because I'm not good at reinventing myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the heavy diesel fitter apprenticeship at the mine in the first year, while the company is still hiring fitters for the new robot trucks. I'd keep saving 500 a month. And I'd put my hand up to be a union delegate, which I've avoided for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's a bit of fight in it. It feels like there's a door, it's just a narrow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not good at reinventing yourself, but you'd start an apprenticeship. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, fair. A fitter is close enough to what I do that it doesn't feel like reinventing, it's the same trucks from the other side. I don't want to become a new person, I just want to be the one fixing the truck instead of the one replaced by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas about the plans you two have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomas we should hold off on buying a house until I'm qualified. He wants to buy next year near the hospital. I'd rather rent a bit longer than have a mortgage while I'm on apprentice pay.

say: I'd tell the union we have **five years** and should use them.
I'd push for a **retraining law** and a proper **redundancy fund**.
I'd say the problem isn't robots but **who owns them**.
think: Robots arrive around **2034**, when I'm thirty-five, which leaves time for a trade.
I'm hoping **someone higher up** sorts it, because reinventing myself isn't my strength.
do: Apply for the **diesel fitter apprenticeship** while the mine still hires fitters.
Keep saving **500 a month** through the apprenticeship years.
Stand as a **union delegate**, a role I've avoided for years.
feel: **Worried**, but with some fight, like finding a **narrow door**.
S3.quote: I don't want to become a new person, I just want to be the one fixing the truck instead of the one replaced by it.
fieldNote: She sees fitting as **the same trucks** from the other side, not a reinvention.
She'd **delay buying a house** with her partner to cope with apprentice pay.
Her **politics** shape the blame: owners of machines, not the machines themselves.

steps.text: Apply for the mine's diesel fitter apprenticeship in year one
Stand for election as the crew's union delegate
Hold off buying a house with Tomas until qualified
Keep saving 500 a month during apprentice pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly if governments actually try. I'd say every mining town needs a plan, not just a press release. I'd say it at work and I'd say it at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd probably waste the first few years, because ten years feels far away and I hate change. By 2039 I'd be thirty-nine, which is old enough to be stuck and young enough to need another twenty-five years of work. That's the trap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving for now, I won't lie, and keep saving 400 a month like now. But I'd set myself a date, say 2030, to have a trade started, and I'd write it on the fridge so Tomas can nag me. I'd keep up the union work on a transition plan for the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but a lazy kind of calm that I don't fully trust. It's the picture where I'd most likely let it creep up on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start, rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing someone I know lose their job. When the north pit lost drivers, nobody I knew personally went, so it didn't feel real. My fridge has a date on it for 2030, and my partner Tomas is allowed to nag me if I'm still driving trucks after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself in 2040?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fixing machines, if I'm smart about it, maybe at the same mine. If I'm not, maybe working in town for less money and being bitter about it. I'd like to be the first one.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough if governments **actually try**.
I'd say every mining town needs a **real plan**, not a press release.
think: I'd probably **waste the first years**, because ten years feels far and I hate change.
At **thirty-nine** I'd be settled, yet still need twenty-five more working years.
do: Keep driving trucks for now and save **400 a month**.
Set **2030** as the deadline to start a trade, written on the fridge.
Keep up the **union work** on a transition plan for the town.
feel: **Calmer**, but a lazy calm I don't fully **trust**.
S4.quote: My fridge has a date on it for 2030, and my partner Tomas is allowed to nag me if I'm still driving trucks after that.
fieldNote: More time makes her **more likely to delay**, and she knows it.
She needs to see **someone she knows** lose a job before it feels real.
A **fridge deadline** and her partner's nagging are her plan against drifting.

steps.text: Keep driving haul trucks at the iron ore pit
Write a 2030 start date for a trade on the fridge
Push a mining-town transition plan through the union

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. The two years means there's no time to finish a trade before the robots come for the cab. What would help is the company paying for apprenticeships while we still earn, and a law that says they have to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women on site. There aren't many of us in the trucks, and if the jobs shrink, I think we're the first to be pushed out. I fought to get into a haul truck cab at twenty, and I'm not ready to hand my seat to a robot at thirty.

headlineQuote: I fought to get into a haul truck cab at twenty, and I'm not ready to hand my seat to a robot at thirty.
portrait: Vera, 27, drives **haul truck 47** at a large open-pit iron ore mine near Redhill.
She lives with **Tomas**, a hospital nurse, and has about **three months** of savings.
She's strongly **pro-union** and blames owners, not machines, for lost jobs.
She **avoids AI tools** and would rather retrain as a diesel fitter.
Her mood darkens with the **two-year warning**, and she fears drifting with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time to finish a trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Company-paid apprenticeships** while still earning, backed by a **law**.
